name: Blasius Friction Factor
description: Computes the Darcy friction factor for smooth-pipe turbulent flow via the Blasius correlation, 0.316*Re^(-0.25), as a function of Reynolds number Re. It gives the dimensionless resistance used in pressure-drop and head-loss calculations.
notes: Valid for hydraulically smooth pipes with Re roughly between 4000 and 1e5. This is the Darcy (not Fanning) factor, which is four times larger than Fanning.

name: Swamee-Jain Friction Factor
description: Computes the Darcy friction factor from the Swamee-Jain equation, an explicit approximation to the Colebrook equation, using relative roughness eps/D and Reynolds number Re. It avoids the iterative Colebrook solution for turbulent pipe flow.
notes: The log is base 10. Valid roughly for eps/D between 1e-6 and 1e-2 and Re between 5000 and 1e8. Approximates Colebrook to within a few percent.

name: Haaland Friction Factor
description: Computes the Darcy friction factor via the Haaland equation, an explicit approximation to Colebrook using relative roughness eps/D and Reynolds number Re. It gives turbulent-flow friction in a single non-iterative expression.
notes: The log is base 10. Applicable to turbulent flow (Re above about 4000). It is typically accurate to within about 2 percent of the implicit Colebrook result.

name: Grashof Number
description: Computes the Grashof number, g*beta*(Ts - Tinf)*L^3/nu^2, the dimensionless ratio of buoyancy to viscous forces in natural convection. It characterizes how strongly a temperature difference drives buoyant flow along a surface of length L.
notes: beta is the thermal expansion coefficient (1/T for an ideal gas). Ts - Tinf is the surface-to-fluid temperature difference. Large Grashof numbers signal transition to turbulent free convection.

name: Rayleigh Number (Natural Convection)
description: Computes the Rayleigh number, g*beta*(Ts - Tinf)*L^3/(nu*alpha), the product of the Grashof and Prandtl numbers governing natural convection. It measures whether heat transfer across a fluid layer is dominated by conduction or by buoyant convection.
notes: Below a critical value (about 1708 for a heated layer) heat moves by conduction; above it convection cells form. alpha is thermal diffusivity, nu kinematic viscosity.

name: Dittus-Boelter Nusselt Number
description: Computes the Nusselt number for turbulent flow in a tube using the Dittus-Boelter correlation, 0.023*Re^0.8*Pr^0.4, from the Reynolds and Prandtl numbers. The Nusselt number gives convective relative to conductive heat transfer for finding the heat transfer coefficient.
notes: The exponent 0.4 on Pr applies to heating of the fluid; use 0.3 for cooling. Valid for Re above about 10000, Pr from 0.6 to 160, and long tubes.

name: Schmidt Number
description: Computes the Schmidt number, nu/Dm, the ratio of momentum diffusivity (kinematic viscosity) to mass diffusivity. It is the mass-transfer analogue of the Prandtl number, describing the relative thickness of velocity and concentration boundary layers.
notes: Dimensionless. For gases it is near 1; for liquids it is much larger (order 100 to 1000) because mass diffuses slowly compared with momentum.

name: Lewis Number
description: Computes the Lewis number, alpha/Dm, the ratio of thermal diffusivity to mass diffusivity. It compares how fast heat spreads versus how fast a species diffuses, and equals the Schmidt number divided by the Prandtl number.
notes: Dimensionless. A Lewis number of 1 means heat and mass diffuse equally fast, a common simplifying assumption in combustion and evaporation analyses.

name: Stanton Number
description: Computes the Stanton number, h/(rho*u*cp), the ratio of heat actually transferred to a fluid to its thermal capacity to carry heat by convection. It is a dimensionless heat-transfer coefficient equal to Nu/(Re*Pr).
notes: h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, u the flow velocity, cp the specific heat. It links directly to the Colburn analogy between heat and momentum transfer.

name: Colburn j-Factor
description: Computes the Colburn j-factor for heat transfer, St*Pr^(2/3), from the Stanton and Prandtl numbers. It recasts the Stanton number into a form that, by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, equals half the friction factor for many flows.
notes: The analogy jH = f/2 lets friction data estimate heat transfer, and jH = jD links heat and mass transfer. Valid for Pr roughly 0.6 to 60.

name: Bulk Richardson Number
description: Computes the bulk Richardson number, g*beta*dT*L*/u^2, the ratio of buoyancy (stabilizing or destabilizing) to shear-driven kinetic energy in a stratified flow. It indicates whether turbulence is suppressed or enhanced by temperature stratification.
notes: Positive values (stable stratification) suppress turbulence; below a critical value near 0.25 shear can overcome stability and generate turbulence. dT is the temperature difference over length L.

name: Rossby Number
description: Computes the Rossby number, U/(f*L), the ratio of inertial to Coriolis forces in a rotating flow, from velocity scale U, Coriolis parameter f, and length scale L. It measures how strongly planetary rotation influences the flow.
notes: Small values (much less than 1) mean rotation dominates, as in large-scale ocean and atmospheric flows; large values mean rotation is negligible. f is the Coriolis parameter.

name: Ekman Number
description: Computes the Ekman number, nu/(f*L^2), the ratio of viscous to Coriolis forces in a rotating fluid, from eddy viscosity nu, Coriolis parameter f, and length scale L. It characterizes the thickness of the frictional Ekman boundary layer.
notes: Small Ekman numbers mean rotation dominates viscosity, typical of geophysical flows. nu here is an eddy (turbulent) viscosity, not molecular viscosity.

name: Womersley Number
description: Computes the Womersley number, R*sqrt(omega*rho/mu), a dimensionless measure of pulsatile flow comparing transient inertial to viscous forces in a vessel of radius R oscillating at angular frequency omega. It describes how the velocity profile responds to unsteady, oscillating pressure.
notes: Small values (below about 1) give quasi-steady parabolic profiles; large values give flatter, phase-lagged profiles. Widely used for blood flow in arteries.

name: Dean Number
description: Computes the Dean number, Re*sqrt(D/(2*Rc)), characterizing flow in a curved pipe of diameter D coiled at radius Rc. It quantifies the strength of the secondary swirling (Dean) vortices induced by centrifugal effects in curved channels.
notes: Above a critical Dean number, counter-rotating Dean vortices appear and enhance mixing and pressure drop. D/(2*Rc) is the curvature ratio.

name: Cavitation Number
description: Computes the cavitation number, (p - pv)/(0.5*rho*v^2), the ratio of the margin above vapor pressure to the flow's dynamic pressure. It indicates how likely a flowing liquid is to cavitate, forming vapor bubbles where local pressure drops to vapor pressure.
notes: Lower values mean higher cavitation risk; below a device-specific critical value bubbles form and can cause erosion. pv is the liquid's vapor pressure at its temperature.

name: Pressure Coefficient
description: Computes the pressure coefficient, (p - pinf)/(0.5*rho*vinf^2), the local pressure relative to freestream expressed in units of freestream dynamic pressure. It is the standard dimensionless measure of the pressure field over an aerodynamic body.
notes: Cp = 1 at a stagnation point in incompressible flow; negative values indicate suction (pressure below freestream). pinf and vinf are freestream conditions.

name: Schiller-Naumann Drag Coefficient
description: Computes the drag coefficient of a sphere using the Schiller-Naumann correlation, (24/Re)*(1 + 0.15*Re^0.687), as a function of particle Reynolds number Re. It extends the Stokes law drag into the intermediate Reynolds-number regime.
notes: Valid for spherical particles up to Re of about 1000. At very low Re it reduces to the Stokes result 24/Re; the correction term accounts for inertial effects.

name: Stokes Settling Velocity
description: Computes the terminal settling velocity of a small sphere in the Stokes (creeping-flow) regime, g*d^2*(rhop - rhof)/(18*mu), balancing gravity, buoyancy, and viscous drag. It gives the steady fall speed of a particle of diameter d in a fluid of viscosity mu.
notes: Valid only for very small particle Reynolds numbers (below about 1), i.e. fine particles or viscous fluids. A negative result (rhop < rhof) means the particle rises.

name: Newton-Regime Terminal Velocity
expression: sqrt(4 * g * d * (rhop - rhof) / (3 * Cd * rhof))
description: Computes the terminal settling velocity of a particle in the high-Reynolds Newton regime, sqrt(4*g*d*(rhop - rhof)/(3*Cd*rhof)), where inertial drag with a roughly constant drag coefficient Cd balances net gravity. It applies to large or fast-settling particles.
notes: Cd is roughly constant (about 0.44) for Reynolds numbers between about 1000 and 2e5. Requires rhop greater than rhof for the particle to settle.

name: Shields Parameter
description: Computes the Shields parameter, tauw/((rhos - rho)*g*d), the dimensionless bed shear stress that governs the onset of sediment motion. It compares the fluid's shear stress driving grains to the submerged weight resisting their movement.
notes: Motion begins above a critical Shields value (roughly 0.03 to 0.06 depending on grain Reynolds number). rhos is sediment density, d the grain diameter.

name: Rouse Number
description: Computes the Rouse number, ws/(kappa*ustar), the ratio of a sediment particle's settling velocity to the turbulent upward mixing set by the shear velocity. It classifies whether sediment travels as bed load, suspended load, or wash load.
notes: Large values (above about 2.5) mean bed load; small values (below about 0.8) mean fully suspended wash load. kappa is the von Karman constant, about 0.41.

name: Shear (Friction) Velocity
description: Computes the shear (friction) velocity, sqrt(tauw/rho), a velocity scale formed from the wall shear stress and fluid density. Though not a real flow speed, it sets the scale of near-wall turbulence and appears throughout boundary-layer theory.
notes: tauw is the wall (bed) shear stress. This velocity scale underlies the law of the wall and dimensionless wall units; it is not the actual fluid velocity.

name: Law of the Wall Velocity
description: Computes the mean velocity in a turbulent boundary layer from the logarithmic law of the wall, (ustar/kappa)*ln(y/y0), at distance y from a wall with roughness length y0. It gives the characteristic logarithmic velocity profile of wall-bounded turbulence.
notes: Valid in the logarithmic (overlap) layer, not the viscous sublayer very near the wall. y0 is the height where the profile extrapolates to zero velocity; kappa is about 0.41.

name: Hazen-Williams Head Loss
description: Computes the friction head loss in a water pipe using the empirical Hazen-Williams equation, 10.67*L*Q^1.852/(C^1.852*D^4.87), from length L, flow rate Q, roughness coefficient C, and diameter D. It gives the energy loss commonly used in water-distribution design.
notes: This SI form assumes water near room temperature; the constant is unit-specific. Higher C means smoother pipe. Not valid for other fluids or very cold or hot water.

name: Joukowsky Water Hammer Surge
description: Computes the Joukowsky pressure surge, rho*a*dv, the peak pressure rise from a sudden change in flow velocity dv in a pipe carrying a fluid of density rho with pressure-wave speed a. It gives the classic water-hammer overpressure from instantaneous valve closure.
notes: Assumes the velocity change is faster than the pipe's wave-return time (rapid closure); slower changes give smaller surges. a is the acoustic wave speed in the fluid-pipe system.

name: Korteweg Pipe Wave Speed
description: Computes the speed of a pressure (water-hammer) wave travelling along a liquid-filled elastic pipe. The rigid-pipe sound speed sqrt(K/rho) is reduced by the pipe wall's flexibility, captured by the ratio (K*D)/(Ep*t) of fluid to wall stiffness.
notes: All moduli and pressures must be in pascals and lengths in metres. Thin-wall assumption; a stiffer or thicker wall raises the speed toward the fluid's own sound speed.

name: Borda-Carnot Expansion Loss
description: Gives the head loss caused by a sudden pipe or channel expansion, where the flow decelerates from velocity v1 to v2. The lost energy equals the kinetic energy of the velocity difference, (v1-v2)^2/(2g), expressed as a height of fluid.
notes: Valid for an abrupt (sudden) enlargement, not a gradual diffuser. Velocities are cross-section averages; the result is a head in metres, convert to pressure by multiplying by rho*g.

name: Hydraulic Jump Sequent Depth
description: Uses the momentum equation to find the downstream (sequent) depth after a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel, given the upstream depth y1 and upstream Froude number Fr. The deeper subcritical flow results from supercritical flow slowing abruptly.
notes: Requires Fr>1 (supercritical inflow) for a real jump; at Fr=1 the depths are equal. Applies to rectangular channels with roughly horizontal bed and negligible friction across the jump.

name: Critical Depth (Rectangular Channel)
description: Returns the critical flow depth in a rectangular open channel, at which specific energy is minimum for the given discharge per unit width q. It is the cube root of q^2/g and marks the boundary between subcritical and supercritical flow.
notes: q is discharge per unit width (m^2/s), not total flow. Valid for rectangular channels only; at this depth the Froude number equals 1.

name: Specific Energy (Open Channel)
description: Computes the specific energy in an open channel, the energy per unit weight measured from the channel bed. It is the sum of the flow depth y and the velocity head q^2/(2*g*y^2), where q is discharge per unit width.
notes: q is per unit width (m^2/s). For a fixed q, specific energy has a minimum at the critical depth; two depths (subcritical and supercritical) can share the same energy.

name: Rectangular Weir Discharge
description: Estimates the volumetric flow over a sharp-crested rectangular weir from the head H measured above the crest. Flow scales with the crest width b and with H raised to the 1.5 power, adjusted by the discharge coefficient Cd.
notes: H is the upstream head above the crest, not the total water depth. Cd (about 0.62) lumps in contraction and viscous effects; assumes free, ventilated overfall.

name: V-Notch Weir Discharge
description: Gives the discharge over a triangular (V-notch) weir from the head H above the notch vertex and the notch angle theta. Flow varies with H^2.5 and with tan(theta/2), making the V-notch sensitive at low flows.
notes: theta is the full notch angle in radians; H is measured from the vertex. The H^2.5 law gives high resolution at small heads but the notch must run with a free, aerated nappe.

name: Sharp-Edged Orifice Discharge
description: Computes the flow rate through a sharp-edged orifice from Torricelli's velocity sqrt(2*g*h) times the orifice area A, corrected by the discharge coefficient Cd. It combines contraction of the jet and velocity loss into one factor.
notes: h is the head above the orifice centre; Cd (about 0.61) already accounts for the vena contracta and friction. Assumes a large upstream reservoir and free discharge.

name: Venturi Meter Flow Rate
description: Determines the volumetric flow through a Venturi meter from the pressure drop p1-p2 between the inlet and throat. It applies Bernoulli and continuity, with the area ratio A2/A1 accounting for the upstream velocity and Cd for real losses.
notes: Pressures in pascals and areas in m^2; p1 must exceed p2. Assumes incompressible flow; the area ratio term requires A2 smaller than A1 to keep the root real.

name: Pitot-Static Tube Velocity
description: Recovers flow speed from a Pitot-static tube using the difference between stagnation pressure p0 and static pressure p. From Bernoulli's equation the velocity equals sqrt(2*(p0-p)/rho), where that difference is the dynamic pressure.
notes: Requires p0>p and the correct fluid density rho. Valid for incompressible flow (low Mach); at high speeds compressibility corrections are needed.

name: Bingham Plastic Shear Stress
description: Gives the shear stress of a Bingham plastic fluid, which flows only after a yield stress tau0 is exceeded. Above yield the stress rises linearly with shear rate gamma at slope mu, so total stress is tau0 + mu*gamma.
notes: Valid only once the material is yielding (stress above tau0); below yield it behaves as a solid and this linear form does not apply. mu is the plastic viscosity, not an ordinary viscosity.

name: Power-Law Fluid Shear Stress
description: Computes the shear stress of a power-law (Ostwald-de Waele) fluid as K*gamma^n. The consistency index K sets the scale and the flow behavior index n sets the curvature: n<1 is shear-thinning, n>1 shear-thickening, n=1 Newtonian.
notes: The units of K depend on n (Pa*s^n), so it is not a plain viscosity. Model has no yield stress; gamma is the shear rate in 1/s.

name: Herschel-Bulkley Shear Stress
description: Combines a yield stress and power-law behavior: the Herschel-Bulkley stress is tau0 + K*gamma^n. The fluid flows only above yield stress tau0, after which stress grows nonlinearly with shear rate gamma governed by K and index n.
notes: Valid only when the material is yielding (stress above tau0). Reduces to Bingham when n=1 and to a power-law fluid when tau0=0; K carries units Pa*s^n.

name: Ergun Equation Pressure Gradient
description: Predicts the pressure drop per unit length for flow through a packed bed of particles. The first term is viscous (Kozeny-Carman-like) and the second is inertial, both scaled strongly by void fraction eps and inversely by particle diameter dp.
notes: eps is the bed void fraction (0-1) and dp the particle diameter; u is the superficial (empty-tube) velocity, not interstitial. Sensitive to eps because of the eps^3 terms.

name: Kozeny-Carman Pressure Gradient
description: Gives the viscous (laminar) pressure gradient for creeping flow through a packed bed, 180*mu*(1-eps)^2*u/(eps^3*dp^2). It is the low-Reynolds limit of the Ergun equation, dominant when inertial effects are negligible.
notes: Valid only for slow (laminar) flow through porous media; at higher velocities add the Ergun inertial term. eps is void fraction and u is superficial velocity.

name: Capillary Length
description: Computes the capillary length sqrt(gamma/(rho*g)), the length scale at which surface tension and gravity balance. Below this scale (a few millimetres for water) surface tension dominates and drops stay nearly spherical.
notes: gamma is surface tension in N/m, rho the liquid density. It sets the size of capillary ripples and the meniscus width; it is a material length, not a droplet size.

name: Galileo Number
description: Returns the Galileo number g*L^3/nu^2, a dimensionless ratio of gravitational to viscous forces using kinematic viscosity nu. It characterizes buoyancy-driven or falling-particle flows without needing a velocity scale.
notes: Dimensionless; nu is kinematic viscosity (m^2/s), L a characteristic length. It is the square of a gravity-based Reynolds number and grows rapidly with L (cube power).

name: Archimedes Number
description: Computes the Archimedes number, the ratio of gravitational buoyancy forces to viscous forces for a particle in a fluid. The driving density difference rhop-rho and particle size L set the tendency to settle or fluidize.
notes: Dimensionless; rhop is particle and rho fluid density, mu dynamic viscosity. A negative value (rhop<rho) means the particle rises rather than settles.

name: Morton Number
description: Gives the Morton number, a fluid property group g*mu^4*(rho-rhog)/(rho^2*sigma^3) that depends only on the liquid, gas, and interface. Together with the Eotvos number it fixes the shape of bubbles or drops rising in a liquid.
notes: Dimensionless and independent of bubble size or velocity. sigma is surface tension; because it appears cubed and mu to the fourth power, small property changes shift it greatly.

name: Weissenberg Number
description: Computes the Weissenberg number lambda*gamma, the product of a fluid's relaxation time lambda and the shear rate gamma. It measures how strongly elastic (viscoelastic) effects appear relative to viscous flow in steady shear.
notes: Dimensionless; gamma is shear rate in 1/s. High values signal strong elastic stresses (rod-climbing, die swell). Distinct from the Deborah number, which uses a flow time scale.

name: Deborah Number
description: Returns the Deborah number lambda/tc, the ratio of a material's relaxation time lambda to the observation (flow) time tc. Small values mean the material acts fluid-like, large values solid-like on the chosen timescale.
notes: Dimensionless; both times in seconds. Note it depends on the observation time tc, so the same material can appear liquid or solid depending on how long you watch it.

name: Taylor Number
description: Computes the Taylor number omega^2*R*d^3/nu^2 for flow between rotating cylinders (Taylor-Couette). It measures centrifugal versus viscous forces and predicts the onset of Taylor vortices when it exceeds a critical value.
notes: Dimensionless; omega is angular velocity, R the mean radius, d the gap, nu kinematic viscosity. Definitions of Ta vary between texts, so compare critical values consistently.

name: Kutta-Joukowski Lift per Span
description: Gives the lift force per unit span on a two-dimensional body from the Kutta-Joukowski theorem: rho*U*Gamma. Lift is proportional to fluid density, freestream speed U, and the circulation Gamma bound to the body.
notes: Result is force per unit span (N/m), not total lift. Valid for inviscid, incompressible 2D flow; Gamma has units m^2/s and its sign sets the lift direction.

name: Blasius Boundary Layer Thickness
description: Estimates the laminar boundary layer thickness on a flat plate as 5*x/sqrt(Rex), where x is distance from the leading edge and Rex the local Reynolds number. The layer grows with the square root of distance.
notes: Valid for laminar flow over a smooth flat plate with zero pressure gradient. Rex must stay below transition (about 5e5); it gives the 99% velocity thickness.

name: Boundary Layer Displacement Thickness
description: Computes the displacement thickness of a laminar flat-plate boundary layer, 1.721*x/sqrt(Rex). It is the distance the outer inviscid flow is pushed away by the slower boundary layer, representing the lost mass flow.
notes: Applies to laminar, zero-pressure-gradient flat-plate flow (Blasius). It is smaller than the 99% thickness and is used to correct effective body shape and inlet areas.

name: Boundary Layer Momentum Thickness
description: Gives the momentum thickness of a laminar flat-plate boundary layer, 0.664*x/sqrt(Rex). It represents the momentum deficit in the boundary layer and is directly related to the wall drag on the plate.
notes: Valid for laminar Blasius flow over a flat plate. It is the smallest of the three thicknesses and links to skin friction via the momentum-integral relation.

name: Laminar Skin Friction Coefficient
description: Returns the local skin friction coefficient 0.664/sqrt(Rex) for laminar flow over a flat plate. It is the dimensionless wall shear stress at distance where the local Reynolds number is Rex.
notes: This is the local (not average) coefficient for laminar Blasius flow; the average over length 0 to x is twice as large. Valid only below transition.

name: Turbulent Boundary Layer Thickness
description: Estimates the turbulent boundary layer thickness on a flat plate as 0.37*x/Rex^0.2, from the one-seventh-power velocity profile. A turbulent layer grows faster with distance than a laminar one.
notes: Valid for a turbulent boundary layer (Rex above about 5e5) on a smooth flat plate with zero pressure gradient; it assumes turbulence starts near the leading edge.

name: Poiseuille Hydraulic Resistance
description: Computes the hydraulic resistance of a circular tube in laminar flow, 8*mu*L/(pi*r^4). It relates pressure drop to flow rate (delta p = R*Q) and rises steeply as the tube radius shrinks (fourth-power dependence).
notes: Valid for steady, fully developed laminar (Poiseuille) flow. The r^4 term makes resistance extremely sensitive to radius; halving r raises resistance sixteenfold.
